title: TraceBound: Evaluating Trace-Bounded Context for Token-Efficient Coding Agents

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to test whether restricting agent file access to execution-trace-derived allowlists reduces token consumption. No prior paper explicitly tests this relationship or investigates token consumption reduction through file access restrictions. Papers like [8] and [14] discuss privilege escalation and least privilege principles but do not empirically test the relationship between file access restrictions and token consumption. Therefore, no prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, TraceBound, computes per-task file allowlists from failing-test execution traces (pytest coverage, depth-2 import closure, interface and auxiliary files) and gates agent file reads with hard denial of out-of-allowlist reads. Paper [6] introduces PIEtrace, which traces and virtualizes program execution, generating a stand-alone trace program. While PIEtrace involves execution traces, it does not compute allowlists or enforce file access restrictions based on them. Paper [9] discusses execution trace obfuscation but focuses on obfuscation strategies rather than allowlist generation or access control. Paper [8] introduces a mandatory access control framework for LLM agents but does not use execution traces to derive allowlists. Thus, no prior paper implements a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses FeatureBench Lite (30 feature development tasks) with OpenHands and measures token consumption changes. Paper [20] introduces LongCodeBench, which evaluates coding LLMs at 1M context windows, and paper [23] introduces LoCoBench-Agent, an interactive benchmark for LLM agents in long-context software engineering. Both benchmarks focus on coding agents and long-context tasks, similar to FeatureBench Lite. While the specific benchmark instance differs, the evaluation design — benchmarking coding agents on task performance — is substantively equivalent. Therefore, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM coding agents. Papers [4], [7], [19], [20], and [23] all address LLM coding agents, covering various aspects such as task performance, context compression, repository-level context files, and long-context evaluation. Although the specific sub-problem differs, the general application area of LLM coding agents is well-covered.
